title: Borel monomial basis for finite connected graded commutative bialgebras
statement: Let $k$ be a perfect field [def-weil-field], meaning that every element has a $p$th root if $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$. Let $H=\bigoplus_{i\geq0}H^i$ be a finite-dimensional graded unital associative $k$-algebra with $H^0=k\cdot1$ and $1\ne0$, and $ab=(-1)^{ij}ba$ for $a\in H^i,b\in H^j$. Suppose $\Delta:H\to H\otimes_k H$ is a degree-preserving coassociative unital $k$-algebra map for the signed multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=(-1)^{\deg b\deg c}ac\otimes bd$, and projection $\varepsilon:H\to H^0=k$ obeys $(\varepsilon\otimes1)\Delta=(1\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta=\mathrm{id}_H$. Then there exist an integer $r\geq0$, positive integers $d_1,\ldots,d_r$, homogeneous elements $x_j\in H^{d_j}$, and integers $N_j\geq2$, such that $x_j^{N_j}=0$ for every $j$, and the ordered monomials $x_1^{a_1}\cdots x_r^{a_r}$ with $0\leq a_j<N_j$ form a $k$-basis of $H$. Each such monomial is homogeneous of degree $\sum_j a_jd_j$. For $r=0$ the family consists of the empty monomial $1$. No bound relating the highest nonzero degree to $\dim_kH^1$ is assumed.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, proof, first sentence quoting Borel (1953): generators subject only to anticommutativity and their nilpotence relations. The finite-dimensional homogeneous bounded-monomial formulation, without a top-degree equality assumption.

proof.text: Put $I=\bigoplus_{n>0}H^n$ and $Q=I/I^2$. Finite-dimensionality and the direct-sum grading imply that only finitely many components are nonzero; choose $D$ with $H^n=0$ for $n>D$. Thus $I^{D+1}=0$. A homogeneous basis of $Q$ has homogeneous lifts $u_1,\ldots,u_s$ of positive degrees. These generate $H$: degree induction expresses a homogeneous $h\in I$ as a linear combination of lifts of its degree modulo $I^2$, and every product in that remainder has factors of strictly smaller positive degrees. In particular $Q=0$ implies $H=k$. Each nonzero positive-degree element is nilpotent. We prove the assertion by strong induction on $\dim_kH$; dimension one is $H=k$, with $r=0$.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: For any homogeneous lifts of a basis of $Q$, apply [lem-sfb-graded-bialgebra-coordinate-derivations]. Its finite-dimensionality, connectedness, signed multiplication and counit hypotheses are exactly those of $H$. It supplies the coordinate maps $\partial_i$ with the signed Leibniz identity and $\partial_i(u_j)=\delta_{ij}$. In characteristic zero, an even-degree generator cannot exist: if $N\geq2$ is its least vanishing power, applying its even coordinate derivation to $u_i^N=0$ gives $Nu_i^{N-1}=0$, a contradiction. Every generator is therefore odd, and $2u_i^2=0$ gives $u_i^2=0$. Ordered squarefree monomials span by supercommutation. If there were a relation, choose a monomial of maximal number of factors with nonzero coefficient and differentiate once in precisely its variables, in reverse order. Every other monomial is killed because it misses a chosen variable; the chosen monomial gives its coefficient times a sign, hence a nonzero scalar. This contradicts the relation. Thus these monomials are a basis, with all $N_i=2$.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: Now let $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$. For $p=2$, the signed algebra is commutative. For odd $p$, write elements as sums of even and odd parity; every odd element has square zero, and even elements commute with everything. Hence $F(h)=h^p$ is additive, multiplicative, and $p$-semilinear: $F(ch)=c^pF(h)$. (For odd $p$, $F(e+o)=e^p$ and $(o_1o_2)^2=0$ prove multiplicativity.) Since $k$ is perfect, $B=F(H)$ is a unital $k$-subalgebra. It is graded, with $B^{pn}=F(H^n)$ and other degrees zero; for odd $p$ it is concentrated in even degrees. It inherits the coproduct: for a homogeneous $h$, expand $\Delta(h)$ into homogeneous simple tensors of total degree $\deg h$. When $p=2$ these summands commute; for odd $p$, if $h$ is even they also commute, and a summand with two odd factors has square zero. Taking $p$th powers therefore gives $\Delta(h^p)=\sum a^p\otimes b^p\in B\otimes_kB$. For odd $h$ in odd characteristic $h^p=0$. The counit identities and coassociativity restrict to $B$. The tensor inclusion is injective by extending a vector-space basis of $B$ to one of $H$. If $H\ne k$ and $n$ is its smallest positive nonzero degree, $B^n=0$ while $H^n\ne0$; thus $\dim_kB<\dim_kH$.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: Apply the induction hypothesis to $B$ with its inherited grading and coproduct. Write its generators as $v_1,\ldots,v_t$, with vanishing powers $v_j^{M_j}=0$ and basis the ordered monomials $v^b$, $0\leq b_j<M_j$. These generators give a basis of $Q_B=B_+/B_+^2$: their classes span, and a relation between them modulo products would contradict independence of the bounded monomials (products of generators reduce either to zero or to monomials of length at least two). The map $F$ induces a surjective semilinear map $Q\to Q_B$ since $F(I)=B_+$ and $F(I^2)\subseteq B_+^2$. Choose homogeneous $y_j$ with $y_j^p=v_j$. Their classes in $Q$ are independent, since applying $F$ to a relation gives a relation between the classes of $v_j$; perfectness lets us extend them to a homogeneous basis by classes $z_l$ in the kernel of $Q\to Q_B$. This is ordinary basis extension, after twisting scalars by the automorphism $c\mapsto c^p$; it is performed separately in each degree. For odd $p$, every $y_j$ has even degree.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: Choose homogeneous representatives of the complementary classes $z_l$. Since $z_l^p\in B_+^2$, express $z_l^p$ as a homogeneous linear combination of bounded monomials in the $v_j$ of length at least two. Take $p$th roots of the coefficients in $k$ and replace each $v_j$ by $y_j$; the resulting homogeneous polynomial $c_l\in I^2$ satisfies $c_l^p=z_l^p$. Its degree is $\deg z_l$. If $p$ is odd and $z_l$ has odd degree, its $p$th power is already zero and choose $c_l=0$. Replace $z_l$ by $z_l-c_l$. Additivity of $F$ gives $z_l^p=0$, and their classes in $Q$ have not changed. Thus the list $w=(y_1,\ldots,y_t,z_1,\ldots,z_a)$ is a homogeneous minimal generating list, with $y_j^{pM_j}=0$, $z_l^p=0$, and also $z_l^2=0$ for odd $z_l$ in odd characteristic. All entries have positive degree and are nonzero because their classes in $Q$ form a basis.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-graded-bialgebra-coordinate-derivations] to this new list $w$. Each resulting coordinate derivation kills $B$: it kills $p$th powers of even elements by the Leibniz identity, and in odd characteristic all odd $p$th powers vanish. Set $q_i=2$ for odd-degree $w_i$ when $p$ is odd, and $q_i=p$ otherwise. The ordered monomials $w^a$, $0\leq a_i<q_i$, span $H$ over $B$, by reducing even exponents modulo $p$ and using the squares-zero relations for odd generators. They are independent over $B$. Indeed, in a finite relation $\sum_a b_aw^a=0$, choose $a$ with $b_a\ne0$ and maximal $\sum_i a_i$. Apply $\partial_s^{a_s}\cdots\partial_1^{a_1}$. The coefficient elements are killed by all these derivations, so they pass through with at most signs; every different monomial is killed because one exponent is too small. The selected term gives $\pm(\prod_i a_i!)b_a=0$. Each $a_i!$ is nonzero in $k$ because $a_i<p$, a contradiction. This calculation uses only the stated coordinate values and signed Leibniz rule, not commutation of the derivations.

source.place: I Lemma 12.2, printed p.55, first sentence of the proof (Borel structure input); agent-written graded invariant-derivation prerequisite, not a lemma stated in Milne.

proof.text: Combine this $B$-basis with the $k$-basis $v^b$ of $B$. Since $v_j=y_j^p$, its products with the residue monomials are, up to invertible signs, exactly the ordered monomials in the $y_j,z_l$ with $0\leq\deg_{y_j}<pM_j$ and $0\leq\deg_{z_l}<q_{t+l}$. The uniqueness of the expression $n=pb+a$ with $0\leq a<p$ gives each allowed exponent exactly once. Thus they form a $k$-basis. Take heights $pM_j$ for $y_j$ and $q_{t+l}$ for $z_l$; the previous steps proved that the corresponding powers vanish, and all heights are at least two. This completes the dimension induction. In either characteristic the degree of an ordered product is the sum of the degrees of its factors, by repeated use of the graded multiplication law, so the monomial with exponents $a_i$ has degree $\sum_i a_i d_i$. The empty generating list gives the single element $1$.
